title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Correlation is not causation



In economics we usually want to know whether x has a causal effect on y.
A correlation may suggest a causal link, but it cannot prove one.
The rooster crows every morning before sunrise. The two events are highly correlated, but the rooster does not make the sun rise.

. . .
Ceteris paribus means “other relevant factors being equal”, or holding all other factors fixed.
Most economic questions are ceteris paribus questions by nature.








Demand example


What is the effect of a price change on quantity demanded, holding income, the prices of other goods and tastes fixed?
If the other factors are not held fixed, we cannot tell what the causal effect of the price is.




The key question in any analysis: Have we held enough other factors fixed?

title: Introduction to Econometrics
section: Interactive: how an unobserved factor fools us
text:
Interactive: how an unobserved factor fools us
Education → wage, but ability affects both education and wage, and ability is unobserved. Move the sliders:




Try this: (1) set ability → educ to 0; (2) set true effect β to 0 and look at the orange line; (3) turn on the experiment.


Discussion prompts. With β = 0 the naive line still slopes up, because more able people get more schooling. The experiment switch assigns education at random, which breaks the link. This is why randomized experiments are the benchmark.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Example 1: fertilizer and crop yield
Question: What is the effect of fertilizer on wheat yield?

Other factors also matter: rainfall, soil quality, parasites, …
Experiment: divide land into equal plots, apply different amounts of fertilizer to each plot and measure the yield.
This gives a cross-sectional data set, where the unit of observation is a plot.









When does this measure the ceteris paribus effect?


When the fertilizer amounts are assigned independently of other plot characteristics, such as soil quality. We do not even need to observe soil quality. We only need the assignment to ignore it.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
section: Check: fertilizer on the best plots
text:
Check: fertilizer on the best plots

A farmer puts more fertilizer on the best plots. The estimated effect of fertilizer will most likely be…
A) about right
B) too large, because good soil raises yields too
C) too small

Soil quality is positively related to both fertilizer and yield. Part of the soil effect is then attributed to fertilizer, and the effect is overstated. It is the same mechanism as ability in the wage example.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Example 2: the return to education


Question: If a person is given one more year of education, by how much will his or her wage rise, holding everything else fixed?
An ideal (hypothetical) experiment:

A social planner draws a random group of people.
The planner randomly assigns each person a level of education.
Years later, the planner measures their wages.

This is a randomized controlled trial (RCT). Here education would be unrelated to ability.








But…


The experiment is impossible, for ethical and practical reasons. Imagine assigning random schooling to 6-year-olds!




Reality: people choose their education, so

more able people tend to get more education, and
more able people tend to earn higher wages.

It is hard to separate the effect of education from the effect of ability.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Example 3: police and city crime
Question: If a city is randomly given 10 more police officers, by how much would its crime rate fall?

We cannot find two cities that are identical in every respect, and we don’t need to. We need to know whether the data can be treated as if they came from an experiment.
In practice the police force is chosen by city authorities, who look at crime when they make the decision.









Simultaneity


Does the police force affect crime, or does crime affect the size of the police force? The two are determined simultaneously. This is another reason why a simple correlation can be very misleading.







Think – Pair – Share
Name one unobserved factor that could bias the simple relationship between police per capita and crime rate. What is the direction of the bias?

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Randomized controlled trials (RCTs)



Subjects are randomly assigned to a treatment group and a control group.
Because of randomization, the groups are the same on average in every respect, observed or not, except for the treatment.
The difference in mean outcomes then estimates the average treatment effect (ATE).
Used routinely in medicine, and increasingly in economics, psychology and sociology.









The crucial ingredient


Randomization. Without it, the groups may differ systematically (selection bias).





Internal validity: do the conditions for a causal conclusion hold here?
External validity: can the results be generalized to other settings?

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Interactive: why randomization works
Each dot is a person. Motivation is unobserved and raises the outcome. Compare self-selection with a coin flip:




Under self-selection, motivated people choose treatment, and the estimate is about 2 + 1.5 × (imbalance). Under a coin flip, individual assignments may be unlucky, but the histogram centers on 2. That is unbiasedness, which we formalize in Week 3.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
RCT examples


Do diets work?

Randomly assign obese individuals to specific diets (Atkins, Ornish, …).
Record weight and other characteristics before the diet.
Follow the individuals for a year or longer and measure again.
H_0: no difference in average weight; H_1: sticking to the diet reduces weight.


Pakistan Early Child Development Scale-Up Trial

Control group: basic health and nutrition services
Group I: enhanced nutrition
Group II: early child development (coaching, visits)
Group III: both interventions
At 24 months, all three treated groups had significantly higher cognitive, language and motor scores.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Quasi-experiments (natural experiments)
When randomization is not possible:

There is still a treatment group and a comparison group, but without random assignment.
Outcomes can often be measured before and after the intervention.
Program evaluation estimates the effect of a program, policy or intervention.


Widely used quasi-experimental methods, which you will meet in later courses:



Matched-pair analysis
Propensity score matching



Difference-in-differences
Regression discontinuity designs









Where this course fits


In Econometrics I we learn multiple regression, which lets us hold observed factors fixed explicitly. This is our main tool for ceteris paribus analysis with observational data.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
section: Predicting college GPA from high-school GPA
text:
Predicting college GPA from high-school GPA


data("gpa1")
ggplot(gpa1, aes(hsGPA, colGPA)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .6, color = "#1f5fa8") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE,
              color = "#d9622b", linewidth = 1.3) +
  labs(x = "High-school GPA", y = "College GPA")

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Try it: a first prediction

coef(lm(colGPA ~ hsGPA, data = gpa1))

#> (Intercept)       hsGPA 
#>   1.4154336   0.4824346


The estimated line is \widehat{colGPA} = 1.415 + 0.482\, hsGPA.

What college GPA do we predict for a student with a high-school GPA of 3.0?

1.415 + 0.482 \times 3 = 2.862. Next week we will see how these two numbers are chosen (ordinary least squares) and what they mean.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Prediction is not causation

Does this line tell us that raising a student’s high-school GPA by 1 point causes college GPA to rise by 0.48?
A) Not necessarily. Motivation or ability could drive both.
B) Yes, the regression proves it.

Good for prediction does not mean causal. Unobserved factors such as study habits or ability probably affect both GPAs.

title: Introduction to Econometrics
text:
Key takeaways



Econometrics uses theory + data + statistics to measure economic relationships.
Most economic data are observational, so we need special methods.
Economic model → econometric model: choose a functional form and add an error term u.
Data types: cross-section, time series, pooled cross-section, panel.
The central question: can we interpret a relationship ceteris paribus, that is, causally?
Randomization breaks the link between the treatment and unobserved factors.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Warm-up

Recall Week 1. Why can’t we simply compare the wages of people with 12 and 16 years of education to learn the return to education?
A) Because wages are measured in dollars
B) Because we don’t have enough observations
C) Because other factors (e.g., ability) that affect wages may differ between the two groups
D) Because education is a discrete variable

The ceteris paribus condition fails if unobserved factors differ systematically across education levels. Today we give this idea a precise mathematical form: the zero conditional mean assumption E(u\mid x)=0.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
The simple regression model


\Large \color{#14324f}{y} = \color{#1f5fa8}{\beta_0} + \color{#1f5fa8}{\beta_1}\,\color{#14324f}{x} + \color{#c0392b}{u}


y x \beta_0 \beta_1 u


Click each symbol to see its name and role.




Also called the bivariate or two-variable linear regression model.
Goal: explain y by x, and in particular measure how y changes when x changes, holding u fixed: \Delta y = \beta_1 \Delta x \quad \text{if}\quad \Delta u = 0

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Two examples



Agriculture
yield = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, fertilizer + u

\beta_1: the change in wheat yield when fertilizer increases by one unit, ceteris paribus
u: land quality, rainfall, parasites, …




Labor economics
wage = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, educ + u

\beta_1: the change in the hourly wage from one more year of education, ceteris paribus
u: experience, ability, tenure, gender, quality of education, …











Linearity has a price


A one-unit change in x has the same effect on y regardless of the starting value of x. Is the 16th year of education worth the same as the 8th? Probably not. Next week we allow for nonlinearities (logs, quadratics).

title: The Simple Regression Model I
section: When can we trust a ceteris paribus conclusion?
text:
When can we trust a ceteris paribus conclusion?
We need assumptions on how the unobservables u relate to x.


Assumption 1: E(u) = 0

On average, the unobservables are zero.
It is not restrictive: as long as the model has an intercept, we can always redefine \beta_0 so that it holds.


Assumption 2: E(u\mid x) = E(u) = 0

Zero conditional mean (mean independence)
The average of u is the same in every slice of the population defined by x.
This is the crucial assumption.










Zero correlation is not enough


\text{Corr}(x,u)=0 only rules out a linear relationship. E(u\mid x)=0 also implies that u is uncorrelated with every function of x, such as x^2 or \sqrt{x}.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Interactive: slices of the population
Think of u as ability. Does average ability depend on education?




Show the U-shaped case: the correlation is about 0, but E(u|x) is clearly not constant. This is exactly why the assumption is stated as mean independence rather than zero correlation.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Zero conditional mean: two examples



Wage equation
Suppose u is mainly innate ability. Then SLR.4 requires
\begin{aligned} E(abil\mid educ=8) &= E(abil\mid educ=12) \\ &= \dots = 0 \end{aligned}
If more able people choose more education, the assumption fails.



Fertilizer experiment

If fertilizer amounts are assigned independently of land quality: the assumption holds ✓
If better plots get more fertilizer: E(u\mid x) increases with x ✗

title: The Simple Regression Model I
section: Check: when does the assumption hold?
text:
Check: when does the assumption hold?

In which case is E(u\mid x) = 0 most plausible?
A) x = police officers per capita, y = city crime rate
B) x = a scholarship amount assigned by lottery, y = exam score
C) x = years of education, y = wage, u contains ability

A lottery makes x independent of everything else, so it works like an experiment. In (A) cities with more crime hire more police (simultaneity). In (C) ability is correlated with education.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
The population regression function (PRF)
Take the conditional expectation of the model and use E(u\mid x)=0:

E(y\mid x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \underbrace{E(u\mid x)}_{=\,0} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Systematic and unsystematic parts
Under E(u\mid x)=0, the dependent variable splits into two parts:

y = \underbrace{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x}_{\text{systematic part } E(y|x)} + \underbrace{u}_{\text{unsystematic part}}



Systematic part: the part of y explained by x
Unsystematic part: the part of y that cannot be explained by x










Where we are going


The PRF is unknown, because \beta_0 and \beta_1 are unknown. With a random sample, we will estimate it.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
The estimation problem
We have a random sample of size n from the population: \{(x_i, y_i): i = 1, \dots, n\}
The model holds for every observation:

y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + u_i, \qquad i = 1, 2, \dots, n




\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + u_1\\
y_2 &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_2 + u_2\\
&\;\;\vdots\\
y_n &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_n + u_n
\end{aligned}



n equations, 2 unknown parameters, and n unknown errors
We cannot “solve” this system exactly.
We need a principle to choose \hat\beta_0 and \hat\beta_1.

Two routes, one answer:

method of moments
least squares

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Route 1: method of moments
Our assumptions imply two population moment conditions. Since E(u\mid x)=0, we have E(u)=0 and \text{Cov}(x,u)=E(xu)=0:

E(y - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x) = 0, \qquad E\big[x\,(y - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x)\big] = 0


Replace the population expectations with sample averages:

\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i\big) = 0, \qquad
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\big(y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i\big) = 0



That gives two equations in two unknowns. From the first one:

\bar y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \bar x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{\hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x}

Notation: hats mean estimators. \hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1 are functions of the data and change from sample to sample.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
The slope estimator
Substituting \hat\beta_0 into the second condition and using \sum x_i(x_i-\bar x) = \sum (x_i-\bar x)^2 and \sum x_i(y_i-\bar y) = \sum (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y):

\boxed{\;\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)^2} = \frac{\widehat{\text{Cov}}(x,y)}{\widehat{\text{Var}}(x)}\;}





The slope is the sample covariance of x and y divided by the sample variance of x.
Its sign equals the sign of the sample correlation between x and y.



We need variation in x: \textstyle\sum_{i}(x_i-\bar x)^2 > 0 If everyone in the sample has 12 years of education, we cannot learn the return to education.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Check your understanding

A tiny sample: x = (1, 2, 3) and y = (2, 3, 3). Compute \hat\beta_1.

\bar x = 2, \bar y = 8/3. The deviations of x are (-1,0,1) and the deviations of y are (-2/3, 1/3, 1/3). \sum (x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y) = 2/3 + 0 + 1/3 = 1 and \sum (x_i-\bar x)^2 = 2, so \hat\beta_1 = 0.5. Then \hat\beta_0 = 8/3 - 0.5\times 2 = 1.667.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Check: no variation in x

In a sample of 200 workers, all have exactly 12 years of education. What happens when we regress wage on educ?
A) \hat\beta_1 = 0
B) \hat\beta_1 is very large
C) \hat\beta_1 equals the average wage
D) \hat\beta_1 cannot be computed

The denominator \sum (x_i-\bar x)^2 = 0, so the slope is undefined. R would report NA for the coefficient.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Route 2: ordinary least squares
For any candidate line, define the fitted values and residuals:

\hat y_i = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_i, \qquad \hat u_i = y_i - \hat y_i = y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i


OLS chooses the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible:

\min_{\hat\beta_0,\,\hat\beta_1}\; SSR = \sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i\big)^2



First-order conditions:

\frac{\partial SSR}{\partial \hat\beta_0} = -2\sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i\big) = 0, \qquad
\frac{\partial SSR}{\partial \hat\beta_1} = -2\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\big(y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i\big) = 0

These are the sample moment conditions multiplied by -2n, so the two routes give the same estimator.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Interactive: be the OLS estimator
Fit the line by hand by making the red residuals, or their squares, as small as you can. Then reveal OLS.




Class game: ask two students to compete, one on the small data set and one on gpa1. Then switch on the squared residuals. Large residuals dominate SSR, which explains why OLS is sensitive to outliers (Week 13).

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Why squared residuals?



Positive and negative residuals would cancel out if we just added them up.
Squaring gives large errors more weight.
It gives closed-form solutions, which are easy to compute and to study.
Under the assumptions of the coming weeks, OLS has very attractive statistical properties (unbiasedness, efficiency).



Minimizing \sum \hat u_i (not squared) would…
A) give the OLS line
B) not have a unique solution, because any line through (\bar x,\bar y) gives \sum \hat u_i = 0
C) give a line with a steeper slope

Every line through the point of means has residuals that sum to zero, so this criterion cannot pick a slope.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
section: Error vs. residual — don’t mix them up!
text:
Error vs. residual — don’t mix them up!



Error u_i

Belongs to the population model
u_i = y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i
Never observed, because the \beta’s are unknown




Residual \hat u_i

Belongs to the estimated model
\hat u_i = y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_i
Computed from the data after estimation











Population (unknown)
Sample (estimated)




PRF: E(y\mid x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
SRF: \hat y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x


parameters \beta_0, \beta_1 (fixed numbers)
estimates \hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1 (vary with the sample)


error u
residual \hat u



The PRF is unique and unknown. The SRF is its estimate and changes with every sample.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Interactive: one PRF, many SRFs




Preview of Week 3: the SRFs scatter around the PRF, and the average of the slope estimates is close to 0.5. That is unbiasedness. With a larger n they scatter less (variance).

title: The Simple Regression Model I
section: CEO salary and return on equity
text:
CEO salary and return on equity
salary = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, roe + u
salary: annual CEO salary in $1000s; roe: average return on equity over the last three years (%); n = 209 firms.

data("ceosal1")
reg1 <- lm(salary ~ roe, data = ceosal1)
coef(reg1)

#> (Intercept)         roe 
#>   963.19134    18.50119




\widehat{salary} = 963.191 + 18.501\, roe

Interpretation: if the return on equity rises by one percentage point (\Delta roe = 1), salary is predicted to rise by 18.501, that is $18,501, ceteris paribus.







Watch the units!


salary is in thousands of dollars, and roe is in percentage points.

title: The Simple Regression Model I

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Three properties that always hold
These follow directly from the first-order conditions. They hold in every sample and do not depend on any assumption.

Residuals sum (and average) to zero: \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n \hat u_i = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \bar{\hat u} = 0
Residuals are uncorrelated with x: \textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n x_i \hat u_i = 0
The point (\bar x, \bar y) is always on the OLS line, and \bar y = \overline{\hat y}.









Where do they come from?


Properties 1 and 2 are exactly the two first-order conditions. Property 3 follows from \hat\beta_0 = \bar y - \hat\beta_1 \bar x.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
R² — common misconceptions

The CEO regression has R^2 = 0.013. What can we conclude?
A) The regression is wrong and should be discarded
B) roe has no causal effect on salary
C) roe explains only about 1.3% of the variation in salaries. Many other factors matter.
D) The OLS estimates are biased

A low R^2 is common with cross-sectional data and does not make the estimates biased or useless. R^2 measures fit, not causality. Whether \hat\beta_1 is a good estimate of the causal effect depends on E(u\mid x)=0, not on R^2.

title: The Simple Regression Model I
text:
Key takeaways



y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u: the error u holds everything else.
E(u\mid x)=0 is the key to ceteris paribus interpretation. It gives the PRF E(y\mid x)=\beta_0+\beta_1 x.
OLS minimizes the SSR: \hat\beta_1 = \widehat{\text{Cov}}(x,y)/\widehat{\text{Var}}(x) and \hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.
The residuals sum to zero, are uncorrelated with x, and the line passes through (\bar x,\bar y).
SST = SSE + SSR. R^2 measures fit, not causality.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Warm-up: a coefficient that shrinks
gpa1 (141 students): college GPA on the ACT score, with and without high-school GPA.



ACT alone
\widehat{colGPA} = 2.40 + \mathbf{0.0271}\,ACT



ACT and high-school GPA
\widehat{colGPA} = 1.29 + 0.453\,hsGPA + \mathbf{0.0094}\,ACT



The ACT coefficient falls to about one-third after adding hsGPA. Why?
A) Adding a variable always makes the other coefficients smaller
B) High-ACT students also tend to have high hsGPA, so ACT alone picked up part of its effect
C) The second regression uses fewer observations

ACT and hsGPA are correlated (0.35), so alone ACT “gets credit” for hsGPA. Multiple regression compares students with the same hsGPA.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Holding other factors fixed explicitly

In simple regression, SLR.4 requires that all other factors in u are unrelated to x. This is often unrealistic.
Multiple regression lets us control for other observed factors that affect y.




Wage equation
wage = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + \beta_2 exper + u
\beta_1: the effect of education holding experience fixed.



Test scores
avgscore = \beta_0 + \beta_1 expend + \beta_2 avginc + u
Omitting avginc would put it in u, and it is correlated with spending.



Multiple regression also allows more flexible functional forms:

cons = \beta_0 + \beta_1 inc + \beta_2 inc^2 + u \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \frac{\Delta cons}{\Delta inc} \approx \beta_1 + 2\beta_2\, inc

The marginal propensity to consume now depends on income. Here we cannot “hold inc^2 fixed” while changing inc.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
section: The model with k explanatory variables
text:
The model with k explanatory variables


\Large y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_k x_k + u


\beta_0 \beta_j x_1,\dots,x_k u


Click each symbol.



Key assumption, MLR.4 (zero conditional mean):

E(u \mid x_1, x_2, \dots, x_k) = 0

For every combination of the x’s, the unobservables average to zero. For example, in the wage equation average ability must be the same for all combinations of educ and exper.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Same principle, more dimensions
The sample regression function is \;\hat y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \hat\beta_k x_k
OLS chooses the k+1 estimates to minimize the sum of squared residuals:

\min_{\hat\beta_0,\dots,\hat\beta_k}\; \sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - \hat\beta_0 - \hat\beta_1 x_{i1} - \dots - \hat\beta_k x_{ik}\big)^2


This gives k+1 first-order conditions, the sample versions of E(u)=0 and E(x_j u)=0:

\sum_{i=1}^n \hat u_i = 0, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}\,\hat u_i = 0 \quad (j = 1,\dots,k)










Geometry


With one regressor OLS fits a line. With two regressors it fits a plane in 3D space. With k regressors it fits a hyperplane that we can no longer draw.

Interpreting the estimates

#> 1.286327767 0.453455885 0.009426012

Holding ACT fixed, one more point of hsGPA raises the predicted colGPA by 0.453, almost half a point.
Equivalently: take two students A and B with the same ACT score. If A’s hsGPA is one point higher, we predict A’s colGPA to be 0.453 higher.
The intercept 1.29 is the prediction for hsGPA = 0 and ACT = 0. No such student exists, so it has no useful interpretation.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
section: Fitted values, residuals and their properties
text:
Fitted values, residuals and their properties

\hat y_i = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_{i1} + \dots + \hat\beta_k x_{ik}, \qquad \hat u_i = y_i - \hat y_i


\hat u_i > 0: the model under-predicts y_i. \hat u_i < 0: it over-predicts.

The algebraic properties from simple regression carry over:

\sum_i \hat u_i = 0, so \bar{\hat u} = 0 and \bar y = \bar{\hat y}
\sum_i x_{ij}\hat u_i = 0 for every j: the residuals are uncorrelated with each regressor
The point of means (\bar x_1, \dots, \bar x_k, \bar y) lies on the regression plane

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
“Partialling out”
With two regressors, the OLS slope on x_1 can be written as

\hat\beta_1 = \frac{\sum_i \hat r_{i1}\, y_i}{\sum_i \hat r_{i1}^2}

where \hat r_{i1} are the residuals from regressing x_1 on x_2: the part of x_1 not explained by x_2.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Simple vs. multiple regression estimates
Compare \tilde y = \tilde\beta_0 + \tilde\beta_1 x_1 with \hat y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x_1 + \hat\beta_2 x_2. In general \tilde\beta_1 \neq \hat\beta_1, and in fact

\tilde\beta_1 = \hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2\,\tilde\delta_1

where \tilde\delta_1 is the slope from regressing x_2 on x_1.


When are the simple and the multiple regression estimates of the slope on x_1 equal? Select all that apply.
A) When \hat\beta_2 = 0: x_2 has no partial effect in the sample
B) When x_2 has a larger variance than x_1
C) When x_1 and x_2 are uncorrelated in the sample, so \tilde\delta_1 = 0

Both cases make the second term \hat\beta_2\tilde\delta_1 vanish. With gpa1: 0.0271 = 0.0094 + 0.453 \times 0.039.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Goodness of fit
The same definitions as before: SST = SSE + SSR and

R^2 = \frac{SSE}{SST} = 1 - \frac{SSR}{SST} = \big[\text{Corr}(y, \hat y)\big]^2

R^2 is the share of the sample variation in y explained jointly by x_1, \dots, x_k. For gpa1: R^2 = 0.176.








R² never decreases when you add a regressor


Adding a variable can only lower the SSR (or leave it unchanged), so R^2 goes up, even if the new variable is pure noise. So R^2 alone is a poor guide for choosing regressors. We will use the adjusted R^2 and F tests later.






Regression through the origin (\tilde y = \tilde\beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \tilde\beta_k x_k): R^2 can be negative, and the estimators are biased if the true intercept is not zero.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Assumptions MLR.1–MLR.4



MLR.1 · Linear in parameters
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_k x_k + u


MLR.2 · Random sampling
\{(x_{i1},\dots,x_{ik},y_i): i=1,\dots,n\} is a random sample.



MLR.3 · No perfect collinearity
No x is constant, and no exact linear relationship holds among the x’s. They may be correlated, just not perfectly.


MLR.4 · Zero conditional mean
E(u \mid x_1, \dots, x_k) = 0. It fails with a wrong functional form, omitted variables correlated with the x’s, or measurement error.









Theorem 3.1: unbiasedness of OLS


Under MLR.1–MLR.4, \;E(\hat\beta_j) = \beta_j for j = 0, 1, \dots, k.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Your turn: perfect collinearity?



Allowed (MLR.3 holds)


Perfect collinearity (MLR.3 fails)



inc and inc^2 in the same model income in dollars and income in thousands of dollars \log(inc) and \log(inc^2) educ and exper, which are correlated shares of spending on food, housing and other, which sum to 1, plus an intercept expend and avginc with correlation 0.9



Hint: \log(inc^2) = 2\log(inc). And inc^2 is a nonlinear function of inc.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Including an irrelevant variable
Suppose the true model is y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u, but we also include x_3 with \beta_3 = 0 (overspecification).

All estimators remain unbiased: E(\hat\beta_1)=\beta_1, E(\hat\beta_2)=\beta_2 and E(\hat\beta_3)=0.
But the variances of the other estimators can increase (see multicollinearity below).









Omitting a relevant variable is worse


Leaving out a variable whose coefficient is not zero (underspecification) generally makes OLS biased.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Omitted variable bias: the formula
True model: y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u. We omit x_2 and estimate \tilde y = \tilde\beta_0 + \tilde\beta_1 x_1.

Using \tilde\beta_1 = \hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_2\tilde\delta_1 and taking expectations:

E(\tilde\beta_1) = \beta_1 + \beta_2\,\tilde\delta_1
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\text{Bias}(\tilde\beta_1) = \beta_2\,\tilde\delta_1

where \tilde\delta_1 is the slope from regressing x_2 on x_1.








\text{Corr}(x_1,x_2) > 0
\text{Corr}(x_1,x_2) < 0




\beta_2 > 0
positive bias
negative bias


\beta_2 < 0
negative bias
positive bias




The bias is zero only if \beta_2 = 0 or x_1 and x_2 are uncorrelated.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
section: Example: ability bias in the wage equation
text:
Example: ability bias in the wage equation

wage = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + \beta_2 abil + u

Ability is unobserved, so we estimate wage = \beta_0 + \beta_1 educ + v with v = \beta_2 abil + u.

What is the likely direction of the bias in \tilde\beta_1?
A) Upward: \beta_2 > 0 and ability is positively correlated with education
B) Downward: ability lowers wages
C) No bias, because ability is unobserved

More able people earn more (\beta_2>0) and tend to get more schooling (\text{Corr}>0). The simple regression overstates the return to education: part of the ability effect is attributed to education. Being unobserved is exactly what causes the problem.



More than two regressors: if the omitted x3 is correlated with x1 only, all the estimated slopes are generally biased, unless x1 and x2 are uncorrelated.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
MLR.5 and the Gauss–Markov assumptions
MLR.5 · Homoskedasticity: \;\text{Var}(u \mid x_1, \dots, x_k) = \sigma^2
MLR.1–MLR.5 together are the Gauss–Markov assumptions for cross-sectional data. MLR.4 and MLR.5 can be written as

E(y\mid \mathbf x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_k x_k, \qquad \text{Var}(y\mid \mathbf x) = \sigma^2









Theorem 3.2: sampling variances of the OLS slopes



\text{Var}(\hat\beta_j) = \frac{\sigma^2}{SST_j\,(1 - R_j^2)}, \qquad j = 1,\dots,k

SST_j = \sum_i (x_{ij} - \bar x_j)^2 is the total variation in x_j, and R_j^2 is the R^2 from regressing x_j on all other regressors.






Three drivers: the error variance \sigma^2 (↑ var), the variation in x_j (↓ var), and how well the other x’s explain x_j (R_j^2 ↑ var).

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Multicollinearity: the intuition


A firm always runs TV and radio ads in the same weeks. Sales rise in those weeks.

Was it the TV ads or the radio ads? The data never show one without the other.
To separate the two effects we need weeks where one changes and the other does not.
The fewer such weeks, the less information we have, and the noisier the estimates.



Link to the formula
By partialling out, \hat\beta_1 uses only \hat r_{i1}, the part of x_1 not explained by the other regressors. Its total variation is
\textstyle\sum_i \hat r_{i1}^2 = SST_1\,(1-R_1^2)
and this is the denominator of \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1).









Variance inflation factor


VIF_1 = 1/(1-R_1^2): how many times larger \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) is than it would be if x_1 were uncorrelated with the other regressors. A common rule of thumb flags VIF > 10, but there is no strict cutoff.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Interactive: multicollinearity




Suggested sequence: start at 0, then 0.5, 0.9, 0.99 and finally 1. Point to the red lines in the left panel: they are the only variation that identifies beta1. At 0.99 about 2% of the information is left and the variance is about 50 times larger. The right panel shows the negative correlation of the estimates: the data pin down beta1 + beta2 well, but not the split. At 1 there is perfect collinearity (MLR.3 fails). Also stress that multicollinearity does not cause bias.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Estimating \sigma^2 and standard errors

\hat\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum_i \hat u_i^2}{n - k - 1} = \frac{SSR}{n - k - 1}, \qquad
\text{se}(\hat\beta_j) = \frac{\hat\sigma}{\sqrt{SST_j\,(1 - R_j^2)}}


Degrees of freedom: n - (k+1) = observations − estimated parameters. The k+1 first-order conditions put k+1 restrictions on the residuals.
\hat\sigma is the standard error of the regression (SER). It can rise or fall when a variable is added.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
section: Standard errors in R, and in equation form
text:
Standard errors in R, and in equation form

g1 <- lm(colGPA ~ hsGPA + ACT, data = gpa1)
summary(g1)$coefficients

#>                Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
#> (Intercept) 1.286327767 0.34082212 3.7741910 2.375872e-04
#> hsGPA       0.453455885 0.09581292 4.7327219 5.421580e-06
#> ACT         0.009426012 0.01077719 0.8746263 3.832969e-01


The same result, written the way papers report it — standard errors in parentheses under the estimates:

\begin{aligned} \widehat{colGPA} &=  \underset{\small (0.341)}{1.29} + \underset{\small (0.0958)}{0.453}\,hsGPA + \underset{\small (0.0108)}{0.00943}\,ACT \\ & n = 141,\quad R^2 = 0.176 \end{aligned}

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
The Gauss–Markov theorem







Theorem 3.4 (Gauss–Markov)


Under MLR.1–MLR.5, the OLS estimators \hat\beta_0, \hat\beta_1, \dots, \hat\beta_k are the best linear unbiased estimators (BLUE) of \beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_k.







Best: smallest variance
Linear: \tilde\beta_j = \sum_i w_{ij}\, y_i, where the weights may depend on the x’s. OLS has w_{ij} = \hat r_{ij}/\sum_i \hat r_{ij}^2.
Unbiased: E(\tilde\beta_j) = \beta_j


Why it matters: if the assumptions hold, there is no need to look for another linear unbiased estimator.

If MLR.4 fails, OLS is biased.
If MLR.5 fails, OLS is still unbiased but no longer “best” (Week 12).

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Check your understanding

A researcher adds a variable that is highly correlated with x_1 but has no effect on y. What happens to \hat\beta_1?
A) It becomes biased
B) Nothing at all
C) It stays unbiased, but its variance increases because R_1^2 goes up
D) Its variance decreases because the model has more information

An irrelevant variable does not cause bias, but it raises R_1^2 and so \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) = \sigma^2/[SST_1(1-R_1^2)]. There is a trade-off: omitting a relevant variable causes bias, while including an irrelevant one costs precision.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
R toolkit for this topic

res <- lm(colGPA ~ hsGPA + ACT, data = gpa1)   # multiple regression
summary(res)                                      # estimates, se, R^2

# partialling out: the same coefficient on hsGPA
r1 <- resid(lm(hsGPA ~ ACT, data = gpa1))
coef(lm(gpa1$colGPA ~ r1))

# omitted variable bias identity: beta_tilde = beta_hat + beta2_hat * delta
delta <- coef(lm(ACT ~ hsGPA, data = gpa1))[2]
coef(res)["hsGPA"] + coef(res)["ACT"] * delta     # = simple slope on hsGPA
car::vif(res)                                     # variance inflation factors

title: Multiple Regression Analysis I
text:
Key takeaways



Multiple regression holds other observed factors fixed explicitly.
\hat\beta_j is the effect of x_j after partialling out the other x’s.
Under MLR.1–MLR.4, OLS is unbiased. MLR.3 rules out only perfect collinearity.
Omitted variable bias = \beta_2\tilde\delta_1. Its sign follows from the 2\times 2 table.
\text{Var}(\hat\beta_j) = \sigma^2/[SST_j(1-R_j^2)]. Multicollinearity inflates it.
Under MLR.1–MLR.5, OLS is BLUE (Gauss–Markov).

Is a year at a junior college worth a year at a university?
twoyear: \;\log(wage) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\, jc + \beta_2\, univ + \beta_3\, exper + u
jc: years at a 2-year college, univ: years at a 4-year university.

tw <- lm(lwage ~ jc + univ + exper, data = twoyear)


\begin{aligned} \widehat{\log(wage)} &=  \underset{\small (0.0211)}{1.47} + \underset{\small (0.00683)}{0.0667}\,jc + \underset{\small (0.00231)}{0.0769}\,univ + \underset{\small (0.000157)}{0.00494}\,exper \\ & n = 6763,\quad R^2 = 0.222 \end{aligned}



H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 \;\;(\beta_1 - \beta_2 = 0) \qquad\text{vs.}\qquad H_1: \beta_1 < \beta_2


t = \frac{\hat\beta_1 - \hat\beta_2}{\text{se}(\hat\beta_1 - \hat\beta_2)}, \qquad
\text{Var}(\hat\beta_1 - \hat\beta_2) = \text{Var}(\hat\beta_1) + \text{Var}(\hat\beta_2) - 2\,\text{Cov}(\hat\beta_1, \hat\beta_2)

The problem: the covariance is not in the standard output.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text:
The trick: reparametrize the model
Define \theta_1 = \beta_1 - \beta_2, so \beta_1 = \theta_1 + \beta_2. Substituting:

\log(wage) = \beta_0 + \theta_1\, jc + \beta_2\,(jc + univ) + \beta_3\, exper + u = \beta_0 + \theta_1\, jc + \beta_2\, totcoll + \beta_3\, exper + u


twoyear$totcoll <- twoyear$jc + twoyear$univ
tw2 <- lm(lwage ~ jc + totcoll + exper, data = twoyear)


\begin{aligned} \widehat{\log(wage)} &=  \underset{\small (0.0211)}{1.47} - \underset{\small (0.00694)}{0.0102}\,jc + \underset{\small (0.00231)}{0.0769}\,totcoll + \underset{\small (0.000157)}{0.00494}\,exper \\ & n = 6763,\quad R^2 = 0.222 \end{aligned}


The coefficient on jc is \hat\theta_1: \;t = -0.0102/0.0069 = -1.47, one-sided p-value = 0.071.
There is some, but not strong, evidence that a year at a university is worth more than a year at a junior college.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text:
Exclusion restrictions
Unrestricted model with k regressors:

y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3 x_3 + \beta_4 x_4 + \beta_5 x_5 + u \qquad (SSR_{ur},\; R^2_{ur})


H_0: \beta_3 = 0,\; \beta_4 = 0,\; \beta_5 = 0 \qquad H_1: H_0 \text{ is not true}

H_0 imposes q = 3 exclusion restrictions: x_3, x_4, x_5 have no effect on y once x_1, x_2 are controlled for. H_1: at least one of them is non-zero.

Restricted model (impose H_0):

y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u \qquad (SSR_r,\; R^2_r)

Dropping variables can only increase the SSR. The question is whether it increases a lot.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
Multiple Regression Analysis III
section: Example: parents’ education and birth weight
text:
Example: parents’ education and birth weight

ur <- lm(bwght ~ cigs + parity + faminc + motheduc + fatheduc, data = bwght)
r  <- lm(bwght ~ cigs + parity + faminc, data = model.frame(ur))  # same 1,191 babies

Unrestricted model

\begin{aligned} \widehat{bwght} &=  \underset{\small (3.73)}{114.52} - \underset{\small (0.110)}{0.596}\,cigs + \underset{\small (0.659)}{1.79}\,parity + \underset{\small (0.0366)}{0.0560}\,faminc \\ & - \underset{\small (0.320)}{0.370}\,motheduc + \underset{\small (0.283)}{0.472}\,fatheduc \\ & n = 1191,\quad R^2 = 0.0387 \end{aligned}

Restricted model (under H_0: \beta_{motheduc} = \beta_{fatheduc} = 0)

\begin{aligned} \widehat{bwght} &=  \underset{\small (1.66)}{115.47} - \underset{\small (0.109)}{0.598}\,cigs + \underset{\small (0.658)}{1.83}\,parity + \underset{\small (0.0324)}{0.0671}\,faminc \\ & n = 1191,\quad R^2 = 0.0364 \end{aligned}

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text:
The same test in R

linearHypothesis(ur, c("motheduc = 0", "fatheduc = 0"))

#> Linear hypothesis test
#> 
#> Hypothesis:
#> motheduc = 0
#> fatheduc = 0
#> 
#> Model 1: restricted model
#> Model 2: bwght ~ cigs + parity + faminc + motheduc + fatheduc
#> 
#>   Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)
#> 1   1187 465167                           
#> 2   1185 464041  2    1125.7 1.4373  0.238


Parents’ education is jointly insignificant: p-value = 0.24.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text: Interactive: the F test

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text:
Jointly significant, individually insignificant
With highly correlated regressors, each t test can fail to reject while the F test rejects.




Press “Find a puzzling sample”. Both t tests fail to reject (0,0 is inside the blue box) but the F test rejects (0,0 is outside the orange ellipse). Then lower the correlation: the ellipse becomes rounder and the puzzle disappears. Typical case: several measures of firm performance in a CEO salary equation.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text:
Relationship between t and F
For one restriction (q = 1) against a two-sided alternative, \;F = t^2. So the F test adds nothing for a single coefficient, and the t test is more flexible: it allows one-sided alternatives.


A two-sided t test gives t = -2.5. The F test of the same single restriction gives…
A) F = -2.5
B) F = 2.5
C) F = 6.25, with the same p-value as the two-sided t test

F = t^2 = 6.25. Since F is always non-negative, it cannot distinguish the direction: it corresponds to the two-sided t test.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text:
Overall significance of a regression

H_0: \beta_1 = \beta_2 = \dots = \beta_k = 0 \qquad (\text{none of the regressors helps explain } y)

The restricted model is y = \beta_0 + u, with R^2_r = 0:

F = \frac{R^2/k}{(1 - R^2)/(n-k-1)} \;\sim\; F_{k,\,n-k-1}

R reports it at the bottom of summary(): for the birth weight model, F(5, 1185) = 9.55, p-value < 0.0001.







Low R², significant regression


R^2 = 0.039 is small, yet the regressors are jointly highly significant. A low R^2 does not mean the regression is useless.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
section: General linear restrictions: rational house valuations
text:
General linear restrictions: rational house valuations
hprice1: are assessed values rational? If so, once the assessment is known, nothing else should help predict the price.

hr <- lm(lprice ~ lassess + llotsize + lsqrft + bdrms, data = hprice1)


\begin{aligned} \widehat{\log(price)} &=  \underset{\small (0.570)}{0.264} + \underset{\small (0.151)}{1.04}\,lassess + \underset{\small (0.0386)}{0.00744}\,llotsize \\ & - \underset{\small (0.138)}{0.103}\,lsqrft + \underset{\small (0.0221)}{0.0338}\,bdrms \\ & n = 88,\quad R^2 = 0.773 \end{aligned}


H_0: \beta_1 = 1,\; \beta_2 = 0,\; \beta_3 = 0,\; \beta_4 = 0 \qquad (q = 4)

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text:
Rational valuations: the restricted model
Under H_0: \;\log(price) = \beta_0 + \log(assess) + u \;\Leftrightarrow\; \log(price) - \log(assess) = \beta_0 + u

hr0 <- lm(I(lprice - lassess) ~ 1, data = hprice1)
c(SSR_r = sum(resid(hr0)^2), SSR_ur = sum(resid(hr)^2))

#>    SSR_r   SSR_ur 
#> 1.880149 1.821529



F = \frac{(1.880 - 1.822)/4}{1.822/83} = 0.67 \;<\; c_{0.05} = 2.48

Fail to reject: no evidence against rational assessments.







Use the SSR form here


The dependent variable of the restricted model is different (\log(price) - \log(assess)), so the R^2 form of the F statistic cannot be used. In R: linearHypothesis(hr, c("lassess = 1", "llotsize = 0", "lsqrft = 0", "bdrms = 0")).

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
section: A large-sample test: the LM statistic
text:
A large-sample test: the LM statistic
The Lagrange multiplier (score) statistic for q exclusion restrictions needs only the restricted model:

Estimate the restricted model and save the residuals \tilde u.
Regress \tilde u on all the regressors (including the excluded ones). Save its R^2_{\tilde u}.
Compute \;LM = n\,R^2_{\tilde u} \;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\; \chi^2_q\; and reject H_0 if LM > c.

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text:
R toolkit for this topic

library(car)
ur <- lm(bwght ~ cigs + parity + faminc + motheduc + fatheduc, data = bwght)
linearHypothesis(ur, c("motheduc = 0", "fatheduc = 0"))    # F test, exclusion
summary(ur)$fstatistic                                    # overall significance

r  <- lm(bwght ~ cigs + parity + faminc, data = model.frame(ur))  # same sample!
anova(r, ur)                                              # F test via two models

# LM test
aux <- lm(resid(r) ~ cigs + parity + faminc + motheduc + fatheduc, data = model.frame(ur))
LM  <- nobs(aux) * summary(aux)$r.squared
pchisq(LM, df = 2, lower.tail = FALSE)

# linear combination: H0 beta_jc = beta_univ
linearHypothesis(lm(lwage ~ jc + univ + exper, data = twoyear), "jc = univ")

title: Multiple Regression Analysis III
text:
Key takeaways



A linear combination such as \beta_1 - \beta_2 can be tested with a t test after reparametrizing the model.
The F test compares SSR_r and SSR_{ur} for q restrictions: F \sim F_{q,\,n-k-1}.
Variables can be jointly significant while individually insignificant, especially when they are correlated.
Overall significance: F = \frac{R^2/k}{(1-R^2)/(n-k-1)}.
The R^2 form works only when both models have the same dependent variable.
The LM test = n R^2_{\tilde u} needs only the restricted model and is valid in large samples.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
section: Warm-up: is more experience always better?
text:
Warm-up: is more experience always better?
From wage1: \;\widehat{wage} = 3.73 + 0.298\,exper - 0.0061\,exper^2

What does this equation say about the effect of one more year of experience?
A) Each year of experience raises the wage by $0.298
B) Each year of experience lowers the wage by $0.0061
C) The effect depends on how much experience the worker already has, and it gets smaller

With a quadratic term the slope is not constant: \Delta wage/\Delta exper \approx 0.298 - 2(0.0061)\,exper. It is about $0.30 for a beginner, $0.18 at 10 years, and it turns negative after about 24 years. Reading \hat\beta_1 alone is a classic mistake.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
section: What changes when we rescale the data?
text:
What changes when we rescale the data?


Changes

the coefficients and their standard errors
SSR and \hat\sigma if y is rescaled
the intercept


Does not change

t statistics and p-values
R^2 and the F statistic
all substantive conclusions



Rescaling is cosmetic: it is used to avoid long strings of zeros and to make coefficients easier to read.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Interactive: changing the units
Birth weight on cigarettes and family income. Switch the units and watch the table:




ounces to grams multiplies every coefficient by 28.35; cigarettes to packs multiplies the smoking coefficient by 20; income in dollars divides its coefficient by 1000. The t statistics (-5.06 and 3.18) and R-squared never move.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Standardized coefficients
What if we want to compare effects measured in completely different units (pollution, crime, rooms)?
Standardize every variable: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation,

z_y = \frac{y - \bar y}{\hat\sigma_y}, \qquad z_j = \frac{x_j - \bar x_j}{\hat\sigma_j}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\hat z_y = \hat b_1 z_1 + \dots + \hat b_k z_k, \quad \hat b_j = \left(\frac{\hat\sigma_j}{\hat\sigma_y}\right)\hat\beta_j

Interpretation: if x_j increases by one standard deviation, y changes by \hat b_j standard deviations, ceteris paribus.







Also called beta coefficients


The original units become irrelevant, so the \hat b_j can be compared with each other.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Example: house prices (hprice2)

data("hprice2")
lvl <- lm(price ~ nox + crime + rooms + dist + stratio, data = hprice2)
std <- lm(scale(price) ~ scale(nox) + scale(crime) + scale(rooms) +
                         scale(dist) + scale(stratio), data = hprice2)
round(rbind(level = coef(lvl)[-1], standardized = coef(std)[-1]), 4)

#>                     nox     crime     rooms       dist    stratio
#> level        -2706.4326 -153.6010 6735.4983 -1026.8063 -1149.2038
#> standardized    -0.3404   -0.1433    0.5139    -0.2348    -0.2703



One standard deviation more pollution lowers the price by 0.34 standard deviations; one standard deviation more crime lowers it by 0.14.
The effect of pollution is more than twice as large as that of crime, and rooms (0.51) has the largest standardized effect.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
section: Logarithms: a quick reminder and one refinement
text:
Logarithms: a quick reminder and one refinement
For a log-level model, 100\,\hat\beta_j is the approximate percentage change. For large changes use the exact formula:

\%\Delta \hat y = 100\,\big[\exp(\hat\beta_j) - 1\big]


Example (hprice2): \widehat{\log(price)} = 9.23 - 0.718\log(nox) + 0.306\,rooms

One more room: the approximation gives 30.6%. What does the exact formula give? (in %, one decimal)

100[\exp(0.306) - 1] = 35.8\%. The approximation understates the effect when the coefficient is large. It is a biased but consistent estimator of the percentage change.




Rules of thumb: log for positive amounts (wages, prices, sales); levels for years, rates and shares; if y \geq 0 with some zeros, \log(1+y) is an option.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Quadratic models

\hat y = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 x + \hat\beta_2 x^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\frac{\Delta \hat y}{\Delta x} \approx \hat\beta_1 + 2\hat\beta_2 x


The marginal effect depends on x: reading \hat\beta_1 alone is meaningless unless x = 0 is relevant.
\hat\beta_1 > 0,\ \hat\beta_2 < 0: concave (∩). \hat\beta_1 < 0,\ \hat\beta_2 > 0: convex (∪).
Turning point: \;x^* = \left|\hat\beta_1 / (2\hat\beta_2)\right|


data("wage1")
wq <- lm(wage ~ exper + I(exper^2), data = wage1)


\begin{aligned} \widehat{wage} &=  \underset{\small (0.346)}{3.73} + \underset{\small (0.0410)}{0.298}\,exper - \underset{\small (0.000903)}{0.00613}\,exper^2 \\ & n = 526,\quad R^2 = 0.0928 \end{aligned}

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Interactive: quadratic models




wage: the tangent is steep at 0, flatter at 10, flat at the turning point of 24.3 years and negative afterwards. Ask whether we believe wages fall after 24 years of experience: only 28% of the sample lies beyond it, and other variables are omitted here. house prices: the relationship is U-shaped, with a turning point at 4.4 rooms; below it there are almost no observations, so in the relevant range the effect of rooms is positive and increasing.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
section: Turning points: always ask whether they matter
text:
Turning points: always ask whether they matter
hprice2, with \log(price) on \log(nox), \log(dist), rooms, rooms^2 and stratio:

hq <- lm(log(price) ~ log(nox) + log(dist) + rooms + I(rooms^2) + stratio,
         data = hprice2)
round(coef(hq)[c("rooms", "I(rooms^2)")], 4)

#>      rooms I(rooms^2) 
#>    -0.5451     0.0623



\frac{\Delta\widehat{\log(price)}}{\Delta\, rooms} = -0.545 + 2(0.0623)\,rooms
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad rooms^* = \frac{0.545}{0.1246} = 4.4


Going from 5 to 6 rooms: \;-54.5 + 12.4(5) = 7.5\%. From 6 to 7: \;19.9\%.
Fewer than 4.4 rooms happens for a handful of communities, so in practice the effect is positive and increasing.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Models with interaction terms

y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \beta_3\,\underbrace{x_1 x_2}_{\text{interaction}} + u
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\frac{\partial y}{\partial x_1} = \beta_1 + \beta_3 x_2


The effect of x_1 depends on the level of x_2 (and vice versa).
\hat\beta_1 alone is the effect when x_2 = 0, which is often meaningless.


Fix: center the interaction. Replace x_1x_2 by x_1(x_2 - \bar x_2). Then the coefficient on x_1 is the partial effect at the average x_2, and its t statistic tests exactly that effect.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
section: Example: attendance and final exam score
text:
Example: attendance and final exam score
attend (n = 680): stndfnl on attendance rate, prior GPA, ACT, their squares and priGPA \times atndrte.

data("attend")
ai <- lm(stndfnl ~ atndrte + priGPA + ACT + I(priGPA^2) + I(ACT^2) +
           priGPA:atndrte, data = attend)
round(summary(ai)$coefficients[c("atndrte", "atndrte:priGPA"), ], 5)

#>                Estimate Std. Error  t value Pr(>|t|)
#> atndrte        -0.00671    0.01023 -0.65607  0.51201
#> atndrte:priGPA  0.00559    0.00432  1.29382  0.19617



\hat\beta_{atndrte} = -0.0067 with t = -0.66: this is the effect at priGPA = 0, which does not exist in the data.
The partial effect at the mean priGPA = 2.59 is \;-0.0067 + 0.0056(2.59) = 0.0077.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
section: The centered model makes it testable
text:
The centered model makes it testable

attend$pg <- attend$priGPA - mean(attend$priGPA)     # centered
ac <- lm(stndfnl ~ atndrte + priGPA + ACT + I(priGPA^2) + I(ACT^2) +
           atndrte:pg, data = attend)
round(summary(ac)$coefficients["atndrte", ], 5)

#>   Estimate Std. Error    t value   Pr(>|t|) 
#>    0.00774    0.00263    2.93844    0.00341


Now the coefficient on atndrte is the effect at the average prior GPA: 0.0077 with t = 2.94, so it is significant at the 1% level.
Interpretation: for a student with average prior GPA, a 10 percentage point higher attendance rate raises the standardized final score by about 0.077 standard deviations.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Interactive: how the effect varies




Move the slider from 1 to 4: the partial effect of attendance rises with prior GPA, and the confidence band is narrowest near the mean of priGPA, where the data are. At low priGPA the effect is not significantly different from zero. This also explains why the raw coefficient on atndrte (the effect at priGPA = 0) has a t statistic of only -0.66.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Adjusted R^2
R^2 never falls when a regressor is added, so it cannot be used to choose between models with different numbers of regressors.

\bar R^2 = 1 - \frac{SSR/(n-k-1)}{SST/(n-1)} = 1 - (1-R^2)\,\frac{n-1}{n-k-1}


It imposes a penalty for extra parameters and can fall.
\bar R^2 rises when a variable is added if and only if its |t| > 1; for a group, if and only if its F > 1.
Useful for comparing non-nested models, e.g. y = \beta_0 + \beta_1\log(x) vs. y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2.








Two rules


The dependent variable must be the same (y vs. \log y cannot be compared), and a higher \bar R^2 is never a reason to include a variable that theory rejects.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Interactive: adding pure noise




The added variables are random numbers, unrelated to college GPA by construction.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Prediction
We want to predict y at given values x_1 = c_1, \dots, x_k = c_k:

\hat\theta_0 = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 c_1 + \dots + \hat\beta_k c_k \qquad \text{estimates}\qquad \theta_0 = E(y \mid x = c)

How to get its standard error without matrix algebra: write \beta_0 = \theta_0 - \beta_1c_1 - \dots - \beta_kc_k and substitute:

y = \theta_0 + \beta_1 (x_1 - c_1) + \dots + \beta_k (x_k - c_k) + u

Regress y on the centered regressors: the intercept is \hat\theta_0 and R prints its standard error directly.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Example: predicting college GPA (gpa2)

data("gpa2")
g <- lm(colgpa ~ sat + hsperc + hsize + I(hsize^2), data = gpa2)
nd <- data.frame(sat = 1200, hsperc = 30, hsize = 5)
predict(g, nd, interval = "confidence")   # for the average student of this type

#>        fit      lwr      upr
#> 1 2.700075 2.661104 2.739047


\hat y = 2.70 with a 95% CI of [2.66, 2.74] for the average GPA of students with these characteristics.







Where is the interval narrowest?


\text{Var}(\hat y) is smallest at the means of the regressors and grows as c_j moves away from them. Predicting far outside the data is risky.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Predicting an individual outcome
For a new individual, \;y^0 = \beta_0 + \beta_1x_1^0 + \dots + \beta_kx_k^0 + u^0, the prediction error is \hat e^0 = y^0 - \hat y^0 and

\text{Var}(\hat e^0) = \text{Var}(\hat y^0) + \sigma^2
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\text{se}(\hat e^0) = \sqrt{\text{se}(\hat y^0)^2 + \hat\sigma^2}


predict(g, nd, interval = "prediction")   # for one individual student

#>        fit      lwr      upr
#> 1 2.700075 1.601749 3.798402


The interval [1.60, 3.80] is much wider: \hat\sigma = 0.56 dominates \text{se}(\hat y^0) = 0.02. More data shrinks the first term but not \hat\sigma.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text: Interactive: two very different intervals

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Check your understanding

A university wants to predict the GPA of one particular incoming student. Which interval should it report?
A) The confidence interval for E(y\mid x), because it is more precise
B) The prediction interval, because a single student also carries the unobserved u^0
C) Either one: they answer the same question

The CI is about the average GPA of all students with these characteristics. For one student we must also account for their individual u^0, which makes the interval much wider.

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
R toolkit for this topic

lm(wage ~ exper + I(exper^2), data = wage1)          # quadratic
lm(stndfnl ~ atndrte * priGPA, data = attend)        # interaction + main effects
lm(scale(price) ~ scale(nox) + scale(rooms), data = hprice2)   # beta coefficients

summary(m)$adj.r.squared                              # adjusted R-squared

nd <- data.frame(sat = 1200, hsperc = 30, hsize = 5)
predict(g, nd, interval = "confidence")               # CI for E(y|x)
predict(g, nd, interval = "prediction")               # PI for one individual

# turning point of a quadratic
b <- coef(wq); abs(b["exper"] / (2 * b["I(exper^2)"]))

title: Further Topics in Regression Analysis
text:
Key takeaways



Rescaling changes coefficients, not t statistics, R^2 or conclusions.
Beta coefficients make effects comparable across variables.
In quadratic models the effect is \hat\beta_1 + 2\hat\beta_2 x, with turning point |\hat\beta_1/(2\hat\beta_2)|.
With interactions the effect of x_1 depends on x_2; center the interaction to test the effect at the mean.
\bar R^2 penalizes extra regressors and can fall; compare only models with the same y.
CI for E(y|x) ≠ prediction interval for an individual: the latter also contains \hat\sigma^2.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Warm-up: a strange prediction
A bank estimates by OLS: \;\widehat{deny} = -0.080 + 0.604\;(P/I\ ratio), where deny = 1 if the mortgage application was rejected.

For an applicant with a P/I ratio of 0.05 the model predicts -0.05. What does that mean?
A) The applicant will certainly be accepted
B) Nothing sensible: a probability cannot be negative. The straight line is the problem.
C) The model is estimated incorrectly

Nothing is wrong with the estimation: OLS did its job. The problem is the model: a straight line eventually leaves the interval [0,1], while a probability cannot. This is the starting point for logit and probit.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
When y is binary
y \in \{0, 1\}: in the labor force or not, mortgage denied or not, owns a house or not, defaults or not. y = 1 is called a success.
Since y takes only the values 0 and 1,

E(y \mid \mathbf x) = 1\cdot P(y = 1\mid \mathbf x) + 0\cdot P(y=0\mid \mathbf x) = P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf x) \equiv p(\mathbf x)


So the usual regression assumption becomes a model for a probability:

\boxed{\;P(y = 1\mid \mathbf x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_k x_k\;}

This is the linear probability model (LPM). It is estimated by plain OLS.







Interpretation


\beta_j = \dfrac{\Delta P(y=1\mid \mathbf x)}{\Delta x_j}: the change in the probability of success for a one-unit increase in x_j, ceteris paribus. The fitted value \hat y is a predicted probability.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
section: Example: married women’s labor force participation
text:
Example: married women’s labor force participation
mroz (n = 753, 1975): inlf = 1 if the woman worked for a wage outside the home.

lpm <- lm(inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + exper + I(exper^2) + age + kidslt6 + kidsge6,
          data = mroz)


\begin{aligned} \widehat{inlf} &=  \underset{\small (0.154)}{0.586} - \underset{\small (0.00145)}{0.00341}\,nwifeinc + \underset{\small (0.00738)}{0.0380}\,educ + \underset{\small (0.00567)}{0.0395}\,exper \\ & - \underset{\small (0.000185)}{0.000596}\,exper^2 - \underset{\small (0.00248)}{0.0161}\,age - \underset{\small (0.0335)}{0.262}\,kidslt6 + \underset{\small (0.0132)}{0.0130}\,kidsge6 \\ & n = 753,\quad R^2 = 0.264 \end{aligned}

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Interpreting the LPM



educ: one more year of schooling raises the participation probability by 0.038, that is 3.8 percentage points, ceteris paribus.
nwifeinc is in $1,000s: $10,000 more husband’s income lowers the probability by 10 \times 0.0034 = 0.034, i.e. 3.4 pp.
kidslt6: one more young child lowers it by 26.2 pp. kidsge6 is insignificant.









Percentage points, not percent


A coefficient of 0.038 means +3.8 percentage points (e.g. from 50% to 53.8%), not “3.8% more likely”.






Two women differ only in that one has one more child under six. By how much does the model say their participation probabilities differ?

0.262, i.e. 26.2 percentage points. The model assumes this is the same whether the change is from 0 to 1 child or from 3 to 4, which is not realistic.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Problem 1: predictions outside [0, 1]




Switch between the two panels. First: 16 women have negative predicted probabilities and 17 above one, out of 753. Second: the residual variance follows p(1-p) closely, so the LPM is always heteroskedastic.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Problem 2: constant marginal effects
The LPM forces the effect of x_j to be the same everywhere:

going from 0 to 1 young child lowers participation by 26.2 pp,
and so does going from 3 to 4.

It is far more plausible that the first child has a large effect and later children smaller ones. Push the model far enough and it must leave [0,1].








Why the LPM still survives


Near the middle of the data the straight line is often a good approximation. In mroz, 96% of the women have no child under six or exactly one, so the coefficient on kidslt6 is mostly the effect of the first child. Just do not extrapolate.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Problem 3: heteroskedasticity
For a Bernoulli variable, the variance is determined by the mean:

\text{Var}(y \mid \mathbf x) = \text{Var}(u\mid \mathbf x) = p(\mathbf x)\,[1 - p(\mathbf x)]

Since p(\mathbf x) changes with \mathbf x, MLR.5 always fails in the LPM.

OLS is still unbiased and consistent (MLR.1–4 can hold), but it is no longer BLUE.
The usual standard errors are invalid: always use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (Week 12), or weighted least squares with \hat h_i = \hat y_i(1-\hat y_i).


coeftest(lpm, vcov = vcovHC(lpm, type = "HC1"))   # lmtest + sandwich

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Keeping probabilities between 0 and 1
Replace the straight line by a function G(\cdot) that always returns a number between 0 and 1:

P(y = 1 \mid \mathbf x) = G(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \dots + \beta_kx_k)




Logit
G(z) = \Lambda(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}
the logistic cdf



Probit
G(z) = \Phi(z)
the standard normal cdf


Both are S-shaped (sigmoid) and strictly increasing. They are estimated by maximum likelihood, not OLS. The two give very similar fitted probabilities.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Interactive: what the likelihood maximizes




Start away from the MLE and watch the two panels. Top: the curve is too flat or too steep and the denied application (red) gets a low probability. Bottom: log L as a function of beta1 with beta0 held fixed, a hill with a single peak. Press “jump to the MLE”: log L = -795.7 at beta0 = -4.13, beta1 = 5.37. Any other pair makes the observed 2,380 decisions less likely.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Interactive: the logit curve




Move beta1: the curve gets steeper, never leaving [0,1]. Move x: the marginal effect is largest at p = 0.5 and vanishes in the tails. This is why beta1 is not a marginal effect, and why we must say “at which x?” when reporting effects.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Example: mortgage applications (HMDA)
2,380 applications in Boston, 1990. deny = 1 if the application was rejected; P/I ratio = payments / income.

lpm_h <- lm(deny ~ pirat + black, data = hmda)
logit_h <- glm(deny ~ pirat + black, data = hmda, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
round(cbind(LPM = coef(lpm_h), logit = coef(logit_h)), 3)

#>                LPM  logit
#> (Intercept) -0.091 -4.126
#> pirat        0.559  5.370
#> black        0.177  1.273



LPM: holding the P/I ratio fixed, being black raises the rejection probability by 17.7 percentage points.
Logit: the coefficients are positive and significant, but 1.27 is not a probability change. We must compute predicted probabilities.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Predicted probabilities

\begin{aligned} \widehat{P(deny = 1\mid \mathbf{x})} &= \Lambda\left( - \underset{\small (0.268)}{4.13} + \underset{\small (0.728)}{5.37}\,pirat + \underset{\small (0.146)}{1.27}\,black \right) \end{aligned}


nd <- data.frame(pirat = 0.3, black = c(0, 1))
round(predict(logit_h, nd, type = "response"), 4)

#>      1      2 
#> 0.0749 0.2241





White applicant with P/I = 0.3: \;\Lambda(-4.13 + 5.37(0.3)) = 0.075, i.e. 7.5%
Black applicant, same ratio: \;\Lambda(-4.13 + 5.37(0.3) + 1.27) = 0.224, i.e. 22.4%


The estimated difference is 14.9 percentage points at this P/I ratio. Note that, unlike in the LPM, the gap depends on the P/I ratio.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
section: Interactive: three models, one data set
text:
Interactive: three models, one data set




Start with the LPM alone and move the P/I slider to a low value to get a negative probability. Then switch on logit and probit: the two curves are nearly indistinguishable. Turn on the black dummy and compare the predicted probabilities for the two groups at P/I = 0.3 (7.5% vs 22.4%).

title: Binary Dependent Variables
section: Marginal effects in logit and probit
text:
Marginal effects in logit and probit

\frac{\partial P(y=1\mid \mathbf x)}{\partial x_j} = g(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \dots + \beta_kx_k)\,\beta_j,
\qquad g(z) = \frac{dG(z)}{dz}


The effect depends on where it is evaluated: the same \beta_j gives different effects at different \mathbf x.
Common choices: the effect at the sample means, or the average partial effect (the average of the individual effects).
The sign of \beta_j and the z statistic can be read directly; the magnitude cannot.


For mroz, the average partial effect of one more year of education is 0.0395 (logit) and 0.0394 (probit) — almost exactly the LPM coefficient, 0.038. Near the center of the data the three models agree.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
section: Inference: z statistics and the LR test
text:
Inference: z statistics and the LR test
Maximum likelihood estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal, so inference works exactly as before, with the normal distribution in place of the t:

z = \frac{\hat\beta_j - a_j}{\text{se}(\hat\beta_j)} \;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\; N(0,1)
\qquad
|z| > 1.96 \Rightarrow \text{reject at 5\%}

R prints z value instead of t value for exactly this reason.

For q restrictions at once there is no SSR to compare, so we compare log-likelihoods instead:

LR = 2\,(\log L_{ur} - \log L_{r}) \;\stackrel{a}{\sim}\; \chi^2_q
\qquad
H_0: \text{the } q \text{ restrictions hold}

Imposing restrictions can only lower the maximum, so LR \geq 0. This is the likelihood-based counterpart of the F test.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Example: are children jointly significant?

f <- inlf ~ nwifeinc + educ + exper + I(exper^2) + age + kidslt6 + kidsge6
ur <- glm(f, data = mroz, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
r  <- update(ur, . ~ . - kidslt6 - kidsge6)          # H0: both coefficients are 0
c(logL_ur = logLik(ur), logL_r = logLik(r))

#>   logL_ur    logL_r 
#> -401.7652 -432.7764



LR = 2\,[-401.77 - (-432.78)] = 62.02 \;\sim\; \chi^2_2,
\qquad c_{0.05} = 5.99,\qquad p < 0.0001


lmtest::lrtest(r, ur)[2, 4:5]     # the same test in one line

#>    Chisq Pr(>Chisq)    
#> 2 62.023  3.404e-14 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Reject H_0: the number of children matters. (kidsge6 alone is insignificant, z = 0.80; kidslt6 carries the joint result.)

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Goodness of fit



Pseudo R^2 (McFadden)
1 - \frac{\log L}{\log L_0}
\log L_0 comes from the model with only an intercept. For mroz: 1 - (-401.77)/(-514.87) = 0.220.



Percent correctly predicted
Predict \tilde y_i = 1 when \hat p_i > 0.5 and compare with y_i. For mroz: 73.6%.









Read the percentage with care


In the HMDA data only 12% of applications are denied. A model that always predicts “approved” is right 88% of the time, and the logit gets 88.3% — almost the same. Always compare with the share of the most common outcome.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Check: reading a logit coefficient

In a logit model \hat\beta_{educ} = 0.22. What can we say?
A) One more year of education raises the probability by 22 percentage points
B) One more year raises the probability by 0.22 percentage points
C) Education raises the probability; the size of the effect depends on the person’s other characteristics

In a nonlinear model the coefficient is not a marginal effect. Multiply by g(\cdot), which is largest for people whose predicted probability is near 0.5.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
LPM or logit?



LPM

estimated by OLS, coefficients are directly interpretable
easy to extend (fixed effects, IV, …) − impossible probabilities, constant effects, heteroskedasticity




Logit / probit

probabilities always in (0,1), effects taper off
the standard tool for classification in machine learning − coefficients need extra work (marginal effects), maximum likelihood










In practice


For effects near the center of the data the two approaches usually agree. Report robust standard errors with the LPM, and predicted probabilities or average partial effects with logit.

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
R toolkit for this topic

lpm <- lm(inlf ~ educ + exper + kidslt6, data = mroz)        # LPM
lmtest::coeftest(lpm, vcov = sandwich::vcovHC(lpm, "HC1"))    # robust se (needed!)

lg <- glm(deny ~ pirat + black, data = hmda, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
pr <- glm(deny ~ pirat + black, data = hmda, family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(lg)

predict(lg, data.frame(pirat = 0.3, black = 1), type = "response")   # probability
mean(dlogis(predict(lg)) * coef(lg)["pirat"])                        # average partial effect
table(actual = hmda$deny, predicted = as.numeric(fitted(lg) > 0.5))  # classification

title: Binary Dependent Variables
text:
Key takeaways



With a binary y, \;E(y\mid \mathbf x) = P(y = 1\mid \mathbf x).
In the LPM, \beta_j is the change in the probability in percentage points.
Problems: predictions outside [0,1], constant marginal effects, and necessary heteroskedasticity → use robust standard errors.
Logit and probit keep the probability in (0,1) with an S-shaped G(\cdot), estimated by maximum likelihood.
Their coefficients are not marginal effects: compute g(\mathbf x\beta)\beta_j or predicted probabilities.
Near the center of the data the LPM is often a good approximation.
